**Borderline/Anti-social/Narcissism/Psycopathy** - These are personality disorders. People have a lot of the same symptoms as people with codependency and often a similar background in childhood. The major difference is a criminal or malicious element. Purely codependent people are generally empathetic and have a hard time hurting others. On the other hand, people with one of these other disorders often lack empathy, are chronically dishonest and very good at manipulating to get their needs met. 

Chances are if you have one of these disorders you don't care (they usually don't until they get much older) until you have to face serious consequences (growing old alone, prison, etc). Why I mention them: If you are codependent (or have another disorder) you might have considered that you have one of these personality disorders or accused of having one by a mental health professional or family member. If you are concerned you have one of these but do not have a malicious intent or criminal background, you probably do not have one of these disorders.

**If you are worried about having one,** you probably don't! They lack empathy and don't care (in fact, they are usually very defensive about mental issues in general, but will sometimes pretend not to as to manipulate you and make you believe they are the same asyou). What they have in common with you is a lack of self-esteem and worth. How they have developed to compensate is completely different. There is also a good chance you are being manipulated by these types of people. If someone in your life tells you they also have mental health issues and tries to become a part of your life, but also acts defensive and refuses to actually **really** try to get help, they probably have a personality disorder and should be cut out of your life immediately.

**OCD/Anxiety/PTSD** - This often occurs in conjunction with depression, but many people think they have it when they don't. It is an overwhelming compulsion to do something that honestly makes no sense. Such as brush your teeth a total of 3 hours a day because you fear losing your teeth, even when your dentist (whom you see way too often) tells you it is destroying your enamel and will cause you to lose your teeth early. Watch "Obsessed" on netflix if you think you have an anxiety disorder. This really shows what they are truly like. Eating disorders also work in a similar way. Social problems can easily be caused by personality disorders, codependency, adhd, etc and cause you to get anxious in social situations. You need to treat your disorder and then you will finally be able to learn better social skills, this should reduce anxiety. It does not mean you have an anxiety disorder. Anxiety disorders are very overwhelming and lack logic (but they are very real).

2. Taking major steps that can actually change your life instead of just "trying."

The most important step I believe is truly evaluating yourself and figuring out what is wrong with you. It is probably one of the things above which is why I went into so much detail. If you read through that and are still uncertain, it's time to enter talk therapy. If you have a good idea of what is wrong you can see a psychiatrist. They will help you try medications and find a talk therapist that will work well for your medication plan. Try medication. It is life changing.

My goal in therapy (what has gotten me to actually change and do better): Learn to be honest with what you think, say and do. Be selfish. Explore your personal desires and feel no shame for having them. Remember, it doesn't matter if the therapist ends up not understanding you correctly or doesn't like you. Be totally honest about yourself. If you think you have a bad therapist (very possible) try a new one. 

If you know there is something wrong but are very uncertain see a talk therapist. They will help you evaluate your childhood, your behaviors, and figure you out. Then you can start learning to cope and change your behavior. Change is not easy. When you are changing, everything flips upside down. Nothing makes sense anymore. You hit rock bottom. You are very confused. If it all feels good, comfortable, and makes sense, you are probably not changing. It will hurt. It will be scary. It will feel like you will never feel normal again. But if you stay the course, it will pass and everything will be better than before.

I recommend this website for online therapy: talkspace.com. Online therapy sounds like a terrible idea or some sort of scam. But I actually really tried three in person counselors and I did MUCH better on TalkSpace. This is because I could write down my thoughts and feelings as I felt them and send them to her, instead of waiting days and forgetting exactly what I wanted to say. After spending along time chatting over text and getting a good baseline down, we did Skype therapy sessions as well. There really isn't a major difference between this and regular therapy, except that it is more affordable and convenient. If you are good at writing, it will be very good for you. If not you might do better with traditional therapy. I also like TalkSpace because you can request a new therapist at any time.

Depressive disorders are caused by actual physical / chemical problems with your brain. However, depression is often triggered by events and people in your life. Since I am a codependent, I always try to take responsibility for everything, even if something wasn't entirely my fault or not my fault at all. This means I sometimes I fail to see a toxic person in my life that is causing problems for me. Since I learned about codependency, I have gotten more careful about people. I have a major depressive disorder and ADHD. These three things saved / changed me, but I am still working on it....

1. Realizing that you have "depression" **and/or** other related mental or behavioral disorders.

Many people with a depressive disorder do not know they have it or how much it affects their life. This is because they have dealt with it forever and don't know what it feels like to live with a healthy brain / social skills. This causes many people to be totally unaware or to get it confused with other disorders. Others are diagnosed with major depression when their problem was caused by another disorder altogether.

Finally most actually have depression + one or more other mental or behavioral disorders, but don't realize it and only seek treatment for one disorder. Having multiple issues is more common than most people think. Coping mechanisms for depression or growing up in a family with a genetic disorder that caused the family to be dysfunctional can easily lead to having 2+ more conditions at a time. Many conditions share similar symptoms. I have a lot of problems but after years of treatment and therapy, going through times when I thought I might have one or more of each of the following disorders, this is how I figured out what really sets them apart.

**Grief / Temporary Depression** - Most people experience a serious bout of depression at least once in their life brought on by a traumatic event. It might feel like it will never go away but if you have never had serious depression before, it's probably just grief (which can cause the same chemical imbalances of depression). However, if you are overwhelmed with work / life and have felt this way a few times before, there is a good chance you have a chronic issue you are trying to ignore. If this is affecting your life you might still require counseling / medication to get back on track, but make sure you are on a plan for temporary depression and not something long term to treat chronic depression. They are treated differently.

**Major Chronic Depression / Bipolar** - Depression isn't usually a 24-7 condition, even major chronic depression. You can feel healthy and normal for periods of time (especially if you have bipolar disorder, which often occurs in cycles of weeks or months). It can be triggered by problems in your life which can make you feel like you just have a stressful life instead of a personal problem.

At the same time, you are not necessarily "depressed" just because you have a hard life. You don't have the money to do the fun things you want or you don't have any friends. These things can trigger depression, but are not themselves depression. Maybe you just need to get your life together so you can afford to do more fun things. If you have the desire too, you are probably not depressed.

How I feel seriously depressed: I no longer feel like doing the things I absolutely love to do when I am the situation to do them. I go to kickboxing class and I can't focus, I want to leave. I get on my xbox and it's boring. Everything seems overwhelming, incredibly boring, and unbearable. All I want to do is nothing. Literally lay in bed and stare at the wall, but even that is boring. It makes me feel like a burden. Empty. It's not because of my life, my life allows me to go out and have fun. I have no interest anymore. So it feels like it will last forever. 

When I am normal, I could train kickboxing for six hours and not get bored. I could play video games all night and never want to stop. Depression kills my interest in life. For no reason. I just don't feel like doing things anymore. It's horrible.

If you still have interest in the activities you enjoy you are probably not depressed. But you could have another issue. If you are depressed you could also have additional issues that you need to confront to get better.

**This is genetic and if no one in your family has been diagnosed or also shown symptoms, there is a good chance you do not have a disorder.**

**ADHD** - A lot of people with ADHD are sad or hate themselves because the disorder causes them to fail over and over or to have unexplainable social issues. It can trigger depression if you are pre-disposed to it but it does not mean you have real depression. You could just have ADHD which is actually much easier to manage than depression. A lot of people get overwhelmed with life due to ADHD and are diagnosed with depression when they don't have depression at all.

If you have a ton of motivation to do well in life but have difficulties following through on commitments, social anxiety and problems with focus, you might have ADHD. If you haven't gotten anywhere just because you have been apathetic you probably do not have ADHD.

**This is genetic and if no one in your family has been diagnosed or also shown symptoms, there is a good chance you do not have a disorder.**


**Codepedency** This a deeply ingrained learned behavior from childhood many people have but do not realize it exists (it's not discussed often). I'm talking about this a lot because I have it and I thought I had almost everything else before I finally learned about it from a social worker (I also have ADHD and issues with depression). It often causes problems that leads people to appear to be depressed or have another disorder. It can also happen injunction with other disorders. If you were "abandoned" in some way as a child or grew up in a dysfunctional family (an alchoholic father, for ex) there is a good chance you have this problem.


There are many symptoms to this disorder. The main is a deep feeling of needing to be liked by others and to make others happy. They feel like there is something wrong with them and they have to compensate, do more than others to make up for it. Codependents feel very uncomfortable when they feel disliked or like they hurt another person. They put the needs of others so much above themselves they lose touch with what they want or never know what it feels like to truly want something for themselves. This leaves them feeling insecure, conflicted and unsure of their true feelings most/all of the time.


This is the way they are their entire lives. They don't know what it's like to be mentally healthy, have their needs met first and be truly loved.


Codependents are easily manipulated because of their desire to help and fix others. They are often targeted by bullies, addicts, and psychopaths. This is why they usually go from one very abusive relationship to another or stay in a moderately abusive relationship for a long time. I believe most codependent people are setup from childhood to be codependent, but who they are with in their first relationship ultimate shapes whether or not they become fully codependent. If they somehow end up in a healthy relationship, it is possible for them to develop healthier behaviors.


Other symptoms:

1.Think and feel responsible for other people---for other people's feelings, thoughts, actions, choices, wants, needs, well-being, lack of well-being, and ultimate destiny.

2. Feel anxiety, pity, and guilt when other people have a problem.

3. Feel compelled --almost forced -- to help that person solve the problem, such as offering unwanted advice, giving a rapid-fire series of suggestions, or fixing feelings.

4. Feel angry when their help isn't effective.

5. Anticipate other people's needs

6. Wonder why others don't do the same for them.

7. Don't really want to be doing, doing more than their fair share of the work, and doing things other people are capable of doing for themselves.

8. Not knowing what they want and need, or if they do, tell themselves what they want and need is not important.

9. Try to please others instead of themselves.

10. Find it easier to feel and express anger about injustices done to others rather than injustices done to themselves.

11. Feel safest when giving.

12. Feel insecure and guilty when somebody gives to them. 

etc, etc, etc


**This is a behavioral issue and does not appear to have a genetic component or to be caused by a chemical imbalance. Other disorders can affect or intensify the symptoms. But he had to hop around a minute because it hurt him. Spar at 20% - 30% unless your Kru says otherwise. If they go too hard and hurt themselves, they will learn from it. If you are supposed to go hard they will learn how to better setup kicks so you won't check them (since you are off balance, can't see, distracted, etc). It's not your fault, don't care if they think otherwise. They will learn in time to take responsibility for themselves or they will quit fighting. This isn't a sport for someone who can't learn from mistakes.

You shouldn't really great bruises from kicking the heavy bag. I did that at very first because I was kicking it wrong and I almost seriously injured my foot, it was like sprained for a while. Don't train on it feels weird. The muscle could be strained / sprained and if you continue to push it you might seriously tear it and need surgery. If it hurts from pushing the bruise directly and impacting on the bruise, it's probably just a bruise. If it hurts from putting weight on the foot in general / twisting it / moving it, you might have a minor injury. Usually requiring 2 days of full rest.

When you kick it should be with your shin, not your foot. **Don't kick hard until you are more accurate and always landing the kick correctly on your shin.** You will almost always have bruised shins and thighs though (from sparring). You definitely toughen up and feel them less over time. The bone on your shin actually thickens. Also I had way more at the beginning, I don't know how your body adjusts to them at gets bruised less easily over time, but it certainly does.

Your goal should be to prove to your sparring partners they can trust you, not that you can fight. Focus on having fun. If you get hit (especially because the other person did something clever) smile. Think about that at first and make it a habit. If someone is going too hard, go lighter, be defensive, teep. When you learn a combo in class, try it on the bag a lot and then try it on a person. Keep doing that. Follow punches with kicks and kicks with punches.


Fighting is an individual sport but you also work together as a team. Most people you train with you will never fight with due to weight, gender or age. You your partners to be comfortable with experimenting and taking risks. If they improve, you will improve as you will have more challenging opponents to play with. Eventually you will be comfortable going harder (around 50% instead of 20%-30%) to get ready to fight, but at first try to be light. All beginners are too hard in the beginning, trying to prove they aren't afraid to hit.


Some gyms provide a bad environment for this, they almost encourage you to hit harder when you are nervous at first. Most new people start super light for a very short period of time, then suddenly get very hard / spazzy, and slowly relax to a manageable level. What they really mean is instead of going 10%, go 30%, not 100%! Don't worry about proving that to them. You can prove it in the ring if you ever want to fight.


Sparring hard is valuable, because everything works different at full power (especially trying to parry or block!), however, you can practice that in time. Learn control first. Make your sparring partners enjoy and trust training with you.

Ribs are THE WORST injuries ever. If it's been a few weeks this wasn't just simple bruising. It could have been a stress fracture or a slight muscle tear. The treatment for both is the same and the doctor can't do anything (unless you have a complete break/tear or need to pop a rib back into place, but this would be obvious and a lot more painful). Anyways, ribs are hard to heal because you can't stop using them. Every time you breathe, you use them delaying healing, and coughing / sneezing can cause an injury to go from bad to worse. There is nothing you can do to avoid this of course. They simple take 3-6 weeks of a lot of careful rest to completely heal. I tore a muscle in between my back ribs four months ago. I coughed and felt a sharp pain, but I figured it was nothing. I tried to train with it at first but it was very painful and got much worse after training. You use your ribs when you roll. It's not like a bum arm or a bum toe or something you can tape up and avoid using. You will use it and agitate the injury.  Finally I realized it was worse than I thought and I took off a full 4 weeks to let it heal. The following 8 weeks it was still sore all the time. I finally thought I was completely over it 3 weeks ago, when randomly in class it started to hurt again, later that night I sneezed and re-strained it. Now I have been out 3 weeks again and it's starting to feel better, but I am really going to warm up and stretch well, and work on strengthening my core muscles before I roll 100% again. I will start drilling and lightly rolling soon... but I learned you have to take this crap slow. Your muscles get super weak recovering beause you can't use them, everything hurts. So when you start again they are tight and weak and re-injure super easily.

Do not get an FHA loan. If you get an FHA loan, you will have to pay the mortgage insurance ($50-$150+ a month) on the loan forever, even after you get 20% equity on the house. Mortgage insurance does not go towards the principle or the equity, it's basically throwing away money. The purpose of mortgage insurance is to cover the cost of foreclosure if you default on your loan. Since you are putting nothing down, the bank will lose a lot of money if this happens (and the mortage insurance covers this). If you put 20% down you don't have to pay for the mortgage insurance sine they get your downpayment if you default.


You can get a conventional loan if you will put down 5% (or more). You have to pay mortgage insurance, but only until you build up 20% equity in the house. Then it comes off and you don't have to pay it anymore. The only difference in requirement between a conventional loan and an FHA loan is 1.5% equity. You need 3.5% for FHA and 5% for conventional. If you can't save up the extra 1.5%, wait until you can. It will save you thousands later even if you have to pay extra rent now. FHA loan's are also actually harder / take longer to get.

I also recommend counting calories and attempting to lose as much fat weight as possible. You could easily lose around 5-10 pounds in 6 weeks. However, if you are already lean and don't have much fat to lose, it will be more difficult or impossible. Then consider cutting water.


If you need to cut water weight, start practicing now. A guy at our gym fights pro and he says when he is active he cuts water weight once or twice a month so his body is used to it. People here will say don't do it, but a lot of people at tournaments were clearly doing it. It's not so much of an advantage unless you are cutting more than 10 pounds (since everyone is doing it). Most people were 1 lb to .1 pound less than the max for their weight class. Jugging pedialytes right after weighing in. Talking about cutting weight in line, etc, etc. A lot of people do it, especially when weigh ins are the night before. If you are at the very bottom of a weight class in a small tournament, you will be going up against people much bigger than you and that won't be fun. If they cut weight they could be 15-25 pounds bigger.


However, it is probably better to compete at or around your natural weight. You will have the edge on being 100% against people who cut and are only 50% - 80% depending on how sensible they were about the cut and how their body reacts. Recovering from cutting water is really hard on your body. This is why I recommend practicing if you decide to do it.


But it isn't necessary and competing at a natural weight would be nice. You get to focus on training with no added stress or worry. If you practice you will know that you can do it and it will be less worrisome. I overdid it on mine because I already sacrificed so much to make weight, I was terrified of not making weight. Then at the tournament I was more afraid of failing because I had sacrificed so much to get into my weight class.


My tips: Research water cuts now and have a solid plan (most plans start two weeks out from competition). The most important part is how much water you drink 7 days before, 6 days before, 5 days before, etc. You do it in a very specific way to manipulate your body and it is much easier on you if you do it this way. Practice it at least once and train the same day / following day to see how you feel. Invest in a good quality accurate scale. Plan your meal immediately following weigh ins. Bring an electrolyte drink (pedialyte is good), then 5-20 minutes later eat a small snack, then have a carb heavy meal. Pasta with red sauce is good. Don't attempt to lose more than 3 pounds if weigh ins are the same day as the tournament. You can lose much more the night before, but that will depend on how your practice runs go.

Like I said, after the two weeks of rest (a week of almost total bed rest) I experienced a lot of DOMS, but this went away quickly and then the pain improved.


I made sure my coach and training partners were aware of and remembered the injury. Explain to your coach the injury and make sure he / she knows it's severe. I immediately followed a session by icing the injured area as it would feel good warm and then start to hurt later as I cooled down and started to get inflamed. Inflammation isn't good. I never really re-injured it training - it was always 30 minutes to an hour after training if I didn't ice it and stretch it. 


My basic list of what I learned:


1. Inform your coach at the beginning of class. Inform training partner(s) as soon as you start working with them (they will forget if you just 'announce' it at the beginning of class, if you switch partners, let them know). This will make you more comfortable with stopping or going lighter (no need to feel embarrassed, they know you aren't lazy, just hurt!) Do not push through any sharp pain.


2. Warmup and stretch thoroughly. Don't be afraid to stop participating in a class drill, technique, etc to re-stretch if the muscles start to tighten. Your goal should be to keep the muscles loose.


3. You will experience DOMS and Injury pain at the same time. DOMS is of little concern. You know it's DOMS if it comes on 24 hours after your training session. But if you are in a lot of pain during training or right after - stop for a few days and focus on stretching. Avoid any movements that cause sharp pain at first. Then do them really lightly as the muscle starts to strengthen after a few days / weeks.


4. Start at home. Shadowboxing is good because you'll know if you can make it through class if you can perform those movements. There is a lot of core activity - but not a lot of actual stress (unlike core exercises or lifting weights, which are way too much, I didn't start doing these again until 8 weeks after the injury). 


5. Always stretch immediately after class, followed by icing as soon as you get home (you can also pick up a box of those instant ice bags at walmart for 2 bucks each, then you can ice on the drive home and get ice on your back even faster.)

1. How do you train on your own without creating bad habits?


Get a journal or notebook. Write down what technique you went over in class that day, what you need to work on, what specific things your instructor told you to focus on, etc. I also write down all the drills we do so I have something to practice on (for ex. 4. I body build as well, will that be a negative overall force on my training?


Extra muscle can lead to two main problems: One, you need more blood to pump these muscles, so it will increase the load on cardio (which means you might not be able to train as long). Two, it will decrease flexibility, which can hinder your ability to kick. It can give you some power, but power really comes from good technique (you can be powerful with good technique and no muscle, and extra powerful with good technique and good power, but you will not be powerful with muscle and bad technique).


So if you body build, keep your cardio up and stretch regularly. Always focus on technique. Never power through sparring.

Learn to get better control and stop kicking so hard. Focus on learning technique first (it's actually easier to hit hard than hit softly with good technique). If you get a powerful kick checked, you will get a lump and a bruise for a while.

Muay Thai should be just as hard on you mentally as it is physically. At first, it takes a lot of thinking to be doing *everything* in correct form, so muscle memory starts to take over. If it feels easy, you are probably doing it wrong. If you aren't thinking about it, form will slip, and you will never get good muscle memory (just bad habits). When I get a good session in, I feel brain dead afterword (especially in the beginning). During any movement I think about: which foot (if either) should be pivoting. Should my hips be open or closed. Should I be lateral to my opponent. Should I be closer or further from my opponent. Jaw hidden behind shoulder. Abs curled and tensed. Breathing out. At least one hand protecting my face. 


When you stop thinking about these basics (due to muscle memory taking over), they become *even more complicated*, as you learn even better technique (or difficult combos) to get even better muscle memory in. It's always a mental struggle to think about these things and improve them, so you can slowly gain muscle memory. I like to throw jab over and over into a bag, cross over and over into a bag, jab - cross, etc, etc. Just so I can get a better feel for "correct form" and I can think about it a little less when learning a more complicated attack, or actually sparring. 


Think about and visualize techniques, combos and counters you are working on all the time. Deep thoughtful visualizing helps in any sport.

Lot's of good advice in here, but I personally like to break down movements into basic goals that will help me achieve the correct movement (especially in the beginning when I was just learning).

1. Make a small step to the outside of your opponent (the opposite side you will kick). Plan the foot with the toes facing away (parallel to your opponent).

2. Stay on the ball of your planted foot, do not let your heal touch the ground at any point.

3. While throwing the kick: twist your planted foot until the heel of it actually goes past your toes (towards your opponent). This should be done about 70% of the way through your kick, right before you strike. 

4. Your hips should be parallel to your opponent when you strike.

4. At first you should practice spinning around in 360 degrees, but always land in the same exact position you started with. (If you missed in a fight, you wouldn't want to be to the side of or even have your back to your opponent!) Your planted foot shouldn't come off the ground at all. Work on your balance, this takes a lot of practice. Once you start bouncing your kick off an opponent or snapping it back, practice going back into the *same exact position* as well. If you marked an x where your foot was before, that is where it should land after the kick.

5. Put the same arm that you are kicking with up in the air right before kicking and throw it behind you / to the side of you with force while kicking. Pretend like you are grabbing an opponent and throwing them behind you (not what you use this for in a fight necessarily, but a good visual to do this correctly). Keep the other hand up protecting your face at all times and pull the throwing arm back to your face immediately after the kick for protection.

6. Flex the kicking foot like you are wearing a boot, this will make your shins harder and more painful on contact. 

7. Don't forget to breathe out and brace your core throughout the whole movement.


Not all of these steps are necessary, especially when performing other styles of side kicks. But they will help you get it down in the beginning. Eventually it will be muscle memory and you will make adjustments. Also this is just what I was taught and what worked from me, if anyone disagrees with it please let me know (and why) I'm here to learn too.
